segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: What advantage, then, does the Jew have, or what is the benefit of circumcision?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Much in every way. First of all, they were entrusted with the oracles of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: What if some were unfaithful? Will their unfaithfulness nullify the faithfulness of God?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: By no means! Let God be true though every person be a liar, as it is written:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “So that you may be vindicated in your words and prevail when you are judged.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But if our unrighteousness brings out the righteousness of God, what shall we say? Is God unjust when he inflicts his wrath? I am speaking in a human way.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: By no means! For then how will God judge the world?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But if through my lie God’s truth has abounded to his glory, why am I also still judged as a sinner?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And why not say—as we are slandered, and as some claim that we say—“Let us do evil so that good may come”? Their condemnation is deserved.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: What then? Are we any better off? Not at all, for we have already charged that Jews and Greeks alike are all under sin,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: as it is written:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “There is no one righteous, not even one;

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: there is no one who understands, there is no one who seeks God.

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: All have turned aside; together they have become worthless. There is no one who does good, there is not even one.

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: Their throat is an open grave; with their tongues they practice deceit; the venom of asps is under their lips.

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: Their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness.

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: Their feet are swift to shed blood;

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: ruin and misery are in their paths,

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: and the way of peace they have not known.

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: There is no fear of God before their eyes.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now we know that whatever the Law says, it speaks to those within the Law, so that every mouth may be shut and the whole world be held accountable to God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For by works of the law no flesh will be justified before him, since through the law comes knowledge of sin.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But now, apart from law, the righteousness of God has been disclosed, attested by the Law and the Prophets—

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ for all who believe. For there is no distinction,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: since all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and are justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: God put him forward as a place of atonement, through faith, by his blood, to demonstrate his righteousness, because of the passing over of sins committed beforehand

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: in the forbearance of God; it was to demonstrate his righteousness at the present time, so that he himself would be just and would justify the one who has faith in Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Where, then, is boasting? It is shut out. By what kind of law? A law of works? No, but by a law of faith.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For we hold that a person is justified by faith apart from works of the law.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Or is God the God of Jews only? Is he not the God of Gentiles also? Yes, of Gentiles also,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: since God is one, and he will justify the circumcised by faith and the uncircumcised through that same faith.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Do we then nullify the law through faith? By no means! Rather, we uphold the law.

notes.note: The Greek verb can mean either “were unfaithful” or “did not believe,” and older versions have the latter. Paul plays on one word-family across verses 2–3: “entrusted,” “unfaithful,” “unfaithfulness” and God’s “faithfulness” all share the root usually rendered “faith.” The contrast with God’s reliability favors “unfaithful,” and most modern translations agree.

Paul quotes Psalm 51:4 in its Greek form (Psalm 50:6 in the Septuagint). The Greek verb form can be passive (“when you are judged”) or middle (“when you go to court”); the Hebrew has “when you judge.” The passive fits Paul’s picture of God being put on trial and winning his case, but the other reading is possible.

Greek has a single word-family where English has two: righteous and just, righteousness and justice, justify. “Vindicated” (verse 4), “unjust” here, “righteous” (verse 10), “justified” (verse 20) and “just” (verse 26) all belong to it. “Righteousness” is kept because “the justice of God” suggests punishing justice to a modern reader, where Paul chiefly means God’s action to put things right. Some scholars prefer “justice” or “covenant faithfulness.”

The single Greek verb is rare in this form and its meaning is disputed. Most translations take it as “Do we (Jews) have an advantage?” It could also be passive, “Are we at a disadvantage?”, or mean “Are we making excuses?” The reply may likewise be “Not at all” or “Not altogether.”

notes.phrase: There is no one righteous, not even one
notes.note: Verses 10–18 are a chain of Scripture quotations, mostly in the wording of the Greek Old Testament: Psalm 14:1–3, Psalm 5:9, Psalm 140:3, Psalm 10:7, Isaiah 59:7–8 and Psalm 36:1. Stringing texts together in this way was a recognized Jewish method of argument. Because these come from the Psalms and Isaiah, “the Law” in verse 19 evidently means the Scriptures as a whole.

The phrase means deeds done in obedience to the Law of Moses. Its focus is disputed: the traditional reading takes it as any effort to gain standing with God by keeping the commandments, while others think Paul has chiefly in view the practices that marked Jews off from Gentiles, such as circumcision, food laws and Sabbath. The verse echoes Psalm 143:2.

The Greek is literally “faith of Jesus Christ,” and the grammar allows two readings: “faith in Jesus Christ” (trust placed in him) or “the faithfulness of Jesus Christ” (his own faithful obedience, through which God’s righteousness comes). The first is the traditional and still majority reading and is followed here; the second has substantial scholarly support.

In the Greek Old Testament this word is the name of the gold cover of the ark, where blood was sprinkled on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16); Hebrews 9:5 uses it that way. The rendering lets that allusion be heard: Jesus is where atonement is made. Whether Paul means the ark’s cover, “propitiation” (turning away wrath) or “expiation” (removing sin) is a long-running dispute.

Older versions join the phrases: “through faith in his blood.” Most modern interpreters take them separately, both describing the atonement: it is received through faith and accomplished by his blood, that is, his death. Some read “through faithfulness,” referring to Christ’s or God’s own faithfulness.

Literally “the one who is of the faith of Jesus.” As in verse 22, the phrase can also be read as “the one who lives from the faithfulness of Jesus,” a reading with substantial scholarly support. The majority reading is followed here.

The word is the one rendered “law” throughout the chapter. Many interpreters think Paul is playing on it here in the looser sense of “principle” or “rule,” and some translations render it so; others think he still means the Law of Moses, viewed either as demanding works or as calling for faith. “Law” is kept so that the reader can see the play on the word.

The Greek word means “nations” or “peoples”; in the plural it was the usual Jewish term for all the non-Jewish peoples. This translation renders the one word as “Gentiles” or “nations” according to the sense.

candidates.reason: Paul shifts between the Mosaic Law, Scripture as a whole and “principle,” and translators differ on rendering and capitalization, so a single policy is needed across the letters.
Recurs throughout the New Testament and could be rendered “grace,” “favor” or “gift”; readers would be misled if it varied without a rule.
Translations vary widely (“flesh,” “human being,” “sinful nature”), and Paul’s usage across his letters needs one consistent approach.
“Redemption” is traditional, but “release,” “liberation” or “ransoming” are plausible, and the word recurs in Paul, Luke and Hebrews.
The verb is central in Romans 4 (“credit,” “reckon,” “count”) and also means “consider”; the senses need fixed renderings so that chapters match.

warnings: Verse 2: πιστεύω is not rendered with a register form (believe / trust) and has no register-exception note.
